claim: RfaH is a transcription regulator of the universally conserved NusG/Spt5 family
source: RfaH, a transcription regulator of the universally conserved NusG/Spt5 family, utilizes a unique mode of recruitment to elongating RNA polymerase to activate virulence genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work on NusG/Spt5 proteins.

claim: RfaH utilizes a unique mode of recruitment to elongating RNA polymerase to activate virulence genes
source: RfaH, a transcription regulator of the universally conserved NusG/Spt5 family, utilizes a unique mode of recruitment to elongating RNA polymerase to activate virulence genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by structural and functional data presented throughout.

claim: RfaH function depends critically on an ops sequence in the non-template DNA strand of the transcription bubble
source: RfaH function depends critically on an ops sequence, an exemplar of a consensus pause, in the non-template DNA strand of the transcription bubble.
evidence: This is supported by the functional assays shown in Figure 2 and prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The ops sequence is an exemplar of a consensus pause
source: RfaH function depends critically on an ops sequence, an exemplar of a consensus pause, in the non-template DNA strand of the transcription bubble.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with consensus pause sequences in Figure 2A and cited literature.

claim: ops induces pausing to facilitate RfaH binding
source: Our results demonstrate that ops induces pausing to facilitate RfaH binding and establishes direct contacts with RfaH.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro transcription assays in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: ops establishes direct contacts with RfaH
source: Our results demonstrate that ops induces pausing to facilitate RfaH binding and establishes direct contacts with RfaH.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure in Figure 4 and NMR data.

claim: The non-template DNA forms a hairpin in the RfaH:ops complex structure
source: Strikingly, the non-template DNA forms a hairpin in the RfaH:ops complex structure, flipping out a conserved T residue that is specifically recognized by RfaH.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure presented in Figure 4.

claim: A conserved T residue is flipped out in the RfaH:ops complex and is specifically recognized by RfaH
source: Strikingly, the non-template DNA forms a hairpin in the RfaH:ops complex structure, flipping out a conserved T residue that is specifically recognized by RfaH.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure in Figure 4C showing T6 flipped into a pocket on RfaH-NTD.

claim: The ops hairpin is required for RfaH recruitment
source: Molecular modeling and genetic evidence support the notion that ops hairpin is required for RfaH recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling in Figure 5A and the double mutant rescue experiment in Figure 5B.

claim: Both the sequence and the structure of the non-template strand are read out by transcription factors
source: We argue that both the sequence and the structure of the non-template strand are read out by transcription factors, expanding the repertoire of transcriptional regulators in all domains of life.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data presented, particularly the hairpin structure and base-specific contacts.

claim: NusG/Spt5 proteins are the only transcription factors that coevolved with RNA polymerase since the last universal common ancestor
source: NusG/Spt5 proteins are the only transcription factors that coevolved with RNA polymerase (RNAP) since the last universal common ancestor (NandyMazumdar and Artsimovitch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: NusG/Spt5 proteins have an N-terminal domain (NTD) of mixed α/β topology connected to at least one β-barrel C-terminal domain (CTD) bearing a KOW motif via a flexible linker
source: These proteins have an N-terminal domain (NTD) of mixed α/β topology connected to at least one β-barrel C-terminal domain (CTD) bearing a KOW motif via a flexible linker.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NusG/Spt5 protein structure.

claim: The NTD of NusG/Spt5 binds across the DNA-binding channel, bridging the RNAP pincers composed of the β' clamp and β lobe domains
source: The NTD binds across the DNA-binding channel, bridging the RNAP pincers composed of the β' clamp and β lobe domains and locking elongating RNAP in a pause-resistant state (Sevostyanova et al., 2011), a mechanism likened to that of processivity clamps in DNA polymerases (Klein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: NusG/Spt5 NTD binding locks elongating RNAP in a pause-resistant state
source: The NTD binds across the DNA-binding channel, bridging the RNAP pincers composed of the β' clamp and β lobe domains and locking elongating RNAP in a pause-resistant state (Sevostyanova et al., 2011), a mechanism likened to that of processivity clamps in DNA polymerases (Klein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional studies.

claim: The mechanism of NusG/Spt5 is likened to that of processivity clamps in DNA polymerases
source: The NTD binds across the DNA-binding channel, bridging the RNAP pincers composed of the β' clamp and β lobe domains and locking elongating RNAP in a pause-resistant state (Sevostyanova et al., 2011), a mechanism likened to that of processivity clamps in DNA polymerases (Klein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an analogy supported by citation.

claim: E. coli NusG binds to termination factor Rho to silence aberrant transcription
source: Escherichia coli NusG binds either to termination factor Rho to silence aberrant transcription (Mooney et al., 2009b; Peters et al., 2012) or to ribosomal protein S10 to promote antitermination (Said et al., 2017) and transcription-translation coupling (Burmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: E. coli NusG binds to ribosomal protein S10 to promote antitermination
source: Escherichia coli NusG binds either to termination factor Rho to silence aberrant transcription (Mooney et al., 2009b; Peters et al., 2012) or to ribosomal protein S10 to promote antitermination (Said et al., 2017) and transcription-translation coupling (Burmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: E. coli NusG binds to ribosomal protein S10 to promote transcription-translation coupling
source: Escherichia coli NusG binds either to termination factor Rho to silence aberrant transcription (Mooney et al., 2009b; Peters et al., 2012) or to ribosomal protein S10 to promote antitermination (Said et al., 2017) and transcription-translation coupling (Burmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bacterial paralogs of NusG, typified by E. coli RfaH, activate long operons that encode antibiotics, capsules, toxins, and pili by inhibiting Rho-dependent termination
source: In addition to housekeeping NusG, diverse bacterial paralogs, typified by E. coli RfaH, activate long operons that encode antibiotics, capsules, toxins, and pili by inhibiting Rho-dependent termination, an activity inverse to that of NusG (NandyMazumdar and Artsimovitch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: RfaH activity is inverse to that of NusG
source: In addition to housekeeping NusG, diverse bacterial paralogs, typified by E. coli RfaH, activate long operons that encode antibiotics, capsules, toxins, and pili by inhibiting Rho-dependent termination, an activity inverse to that of NusG (NandyMazumdar and Artsimovitch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the functional data in the manuscript.

claim: All RfaH-controlled operons have 12-nt operon polarity suppressor (ops) signals in their leader regions
source: Indeed, all RfaH-controlled operons have 12-nt operon polarity suppressor (ops) signals in their leader regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by prior genomic and functional studies.

claim: RfaH is recruited at ops sites in vitro and in vivo
source: RfaH is recruited at ops sites in vitro and in vivo (Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002; Belogurov et al., 2009) through direct contacts with the non-template (NT) DNA strand in the transcription bubble (Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002), a target shared with σ (Sevostyanova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data in this manuscript.

claim: RfaH is recruited through direct contacts with the non-template (NT) DNA strand in the transcription bubble
source: RfaH is recruited at ops sites in vitro and in vivo (Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002; Belogurov et al., 2009) through direct contacts with the non-template (NT) DNA strand in the transcription bubble (Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002), a target shared with σ (Sevostyanova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations and the structural data in Figure 4.

claim: The non-template DNA strand is a target shared by RfaH and σ
source: RfaH is recruited at ops sites in vitro and in vivo (Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002; Belogurov et al., 2009) through direct contacts with the non-template (NT) DNA strand in the transcription bubble (Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002), a target shared with σ (Sevostyanova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: E. coli NusG is associated with RNAP transcribing most genes and lacks sequence specificity
source: However, E. coli NusG is associated with RNAP transcribing most genes and lacks sequence specificity (Mooney et al., 2009a) arguing against an alternative recognition sites model.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Off-target recruitment of RfaH is blocked by autoinhibition
source: In a working model, off-target recruitment of RfaH is blocked by autoinhibition (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a model supported by prior structural and functional studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: RfaH-CTD folds as an α-helical hairpin that masks the RNAP-binding site on the NTD
source: RfaH-CTD, unlike the CTDs of all other known NusG/Spt5 proteins, which adopt a β-barrel structure, folds as an α-helical hairpin that masks the RNAP-binding site on the NTD (Belogurov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: The CTDs of all other known NusG/Spt5 proteins adopt a β-barrel structure
source: RfaH-CTD, unlike the CTDs of all other known NusG/Spt5 proteins, which adopt a β-barrel structure, folds as an α-helical hairpin that masks the RNAP-binding site on the NTD (Belogurov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NusG/Spt5 protein structures.

claim: Contacts with the ops element in the NT DNA trigger domain dissociation, transforming RfaH into an open, active state
source: Contacts with the ops element in the NT DNA are thought to trigger domain dissociation, transforming RfaH into an open, active state in which the NTD can bind to RNAP (Belogurov et al., 2007); consistently, destabilization of the domain interface enables sequence-independent recruitment (Belogurov et al., 2007; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a model supported by prior work, though the NMR data in this manuscript show the domain interface remains intact in the binary complex.

claim: Destabilization of the domain interface enables sequence-independent recruitment of RfaH
source: Contacts with the ops element in the NT DNA are thought to trigger domain dissociation, transforming RfaH into an open, active state in which the NTD can bind to RNAP (Belogurov et al., 2007); consistently, destabilization of the domain interface enables sequence-independent recruitment (Belogurov et al., 2007; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: The α-helical CTD of RfaH spontaneously refolds into a NusG-like β-barrel upon release
source: On release, the α-helical CTD spontaneously refolds into a NusG-like β-barrel (Burmann et al., 2012), classifying RfaH as a transformer protein (Knauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior NMR studies.

claim: RfaH is classified as a transformer protein
source: On release, the α-helical CTD spontaneously refolds into a NusG-like β-barrel (Burmann et al., 2012), classifying RfaH as a transformer protein (Knauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Activated RfaH remains bound to the transcription elongation complex (TEC) until termination
source: Activated RfaH remains bound to the transcription elongation complex (TEC) until termination (Belogurov et al., 2009), excluding NusG present in 100-fold excess (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: RfaH excludes NusG present in 100-fold excess
source: Activated RfaH remains bound to the transcription elongation complex (TEC) until termination (Belogurov et al., 2009), excluding NusG present in 100-fold excess (Schmidt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The β-barrel CTD of RfaH recruits the 30S subunit of the ribosome to leader sequences that lack Shine-Dalgarno elements via interactions with S10
source: The β-barrel CTD recruits the 30S subunit of the ribosome to leader sequences that lack Shine-Dalgarno elements via interactions with S10 (Burmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior NMR and functional studies.

claim: ops matches the consensus pause signal
source: Native-elongation-transcript sequencing analysis revealed that ops matches the consensus pause signal (Figure 2A) and is one of the strongest pauses in E. coli (Larson et al., 2014; Vvedenskaya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations to genome-wide studies.

claim: ops is one of the strongest pauses in E. coli
source: Native-elongation-transcript sequencing analysis revealed that ops matches the consensus pause signal (Figure 2A) and is one of the strongest pauses in E. coli (Larson et al., 2014; Vvedenskaya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome-wide pause mapping studies.

claim: All experimentally validated E. coli RfaH targets share a pause-inducing TG dinucleotide at positions 11 and 12
source: The observation that all experimentally validated E. coli RfaH targets (Belogurov et al., 2009) share a pause-inducing TG dinucleotide (Chan et al., 1997; Vvedenskaya et al., 2014) at positions 11 and 12 (Figure 2A) suggests that delaying RNAP at the ops site may be necessary for loading of RfaH.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: Delaying RNAP at the ops site may be necessary for loading of RfaH
source: The observation that all experimentally validated E. coli RfaH targets (Belogurov et al., 2009) share a pause-inducing TG dinucleotide (Chan et al., 1997; Vvedenskaya et al., 2014) at positions 11 and 12 (Figure 2A) suggests that delaying RNAP at the ops site may be necessary for loading of RfaH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of pause-inducing sequences.

claim: Potential interactions with RfaH are restricted to the central 5–6 nts of ops in the NT DNA strand
source: However, potential interactions with RfaH are restricted to the central 5–6 nts of ops in the NT DNA strand, as these are expected to be exposed on the surface of the ops-paused RNAP (Kang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of the paused TEC cited.

claim: RfaH increases expression of the lux reporter ~40 fold with the wild-type ops
source: To evaluate the roles of individual ops bases in vivo we used a luciferase (lux) reporter system (Burmann et al., 2012) in which RfaH increases expression ~40 fold with the wild-type (WT) ops (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The stimulating effect of RfaH was reduced by every ops substitution except for G2C
source: The stimulating effect of RfaH was reduced by every ops substitution except for G2C (Figure 2B), with the strongest defects observed for substitutions G5A, T6A, G8C, and T11G.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The strongest defects in RfaH stimulation were observed for substitutions G5A, T6A, G8C, and T11G
source: The stimulating effect of RfaH was reduced by every ops substitution except for G2C (Figure 2B), with the strongest defects observed for substitutions G5A, T6A, G8C, and T11G.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: T11 is buried in the RNAP active site
source: Since T11 is buried in the RNAP active site (Kang et al., 2017), the strong effect of the T11G substitution is consistent with the essential role of pausing in RfaH activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a cryo-EM structure.

claim: The strong effect of the T11G substitution is consistent with the essential role of pausing in RfaH activity
source: Since T11 is buried in the RNAP active site (Kang et al., 2017), the strong effect of the T11G substitution is consistent with the essential role of pausing in RfaH activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the position of T11 and the functional data.

claim: On the WT ops template, RNAP paused at C9 and U11
source: On the WT ops template, RNAP paused at C9 and U11.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of RfaH, pausing at U11 was significantly reduced
source: In the presence of RfaH, pausing at U11 was significantly reduced, but strongly enhanced at G12, a well-documented consequence of RfaH recruitment attributed to persistent RfaH-NTD:DNA contacts (Belogurov et al., 2007) and akin to σ-induced delay of RNAP escape from promoters and promoter-like sequences during elongation (Perdue and Roberts, 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and supported by citations.

claim: In the presence of RfaH, pausing was strongly enhanced at G12
source: In the presence of RfaH, pausing at U11 was significantly reduced, but strongly enhanced at G12, a well-documented consequence of RfaH recruitment attributed to persistent RfaH-NTD:DNA contacts (Belogurov et al., 2007) and akin to σ-induced delay of RNAP escape from promoters and promoter-like sequences during elongation (Perdue and Roberts, 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and supported by citations.

claim: Enhanced pausing at G12 in the presence of RfaH is attributed to persistent RfaH-NTD:DNA contacts
source: In the presence of RfaH, pausing at U11 was significantly reduced, but strongly enhanced at G12, a well-documented consequence of RfaH recruitment attributed to persistent RfaH-NTD:DNA contacts (Belogurov et al., 2007) and akin to σ-induced delay of RNAP escape from promoters and promoter-like sequences during elongation (Perdue and Roberts, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: C3G and T6A substitutions reduced RfaH recruitment and antipausing activity ~3 fold
source: While C3G and T6A substitutions reduced RfaH recruitment and antipausing activity ~3 fold, G4C, G5A, A7T, and G8C abolished both effects completely (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: G4C, G5A, A7T, and G8C substitutions abolished RfaH recruitment and antipausing activity completely
source: While C3G and T6A substitutions reduced RfaH recruitment and antipausing activity ~3 fold, G4C, G5A, A7T, and G8C abolished both effects completely (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: None of the central bases (G4, G5, A7, G8) were required for RNAP pausing
source: Neither of these central bases was required for RNAP pausing (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with their variability in the consensus pause sequence (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The G12C substitution eliminated the pause at U11
source: Conversely, the G12C substitution eliminated the pause at U11, making measurements of RfaH antipausing activity unreliable, but did not abrogate RfaH recruitment (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that pausing at U11 is dispensable for RfaH binding when RNAP is transcribing slowly.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The G12C substitution did not abrogate RfaH recruitment
source: Conversely, the G12C substitution eliminated the pause at U11, making measurements of RfaH antipausing activity unreliable, but did not abrogate RfaH recruitment (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that pausing at U11 is dispensable for RfaH binding when RNAP is transcribing slowly.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Pausing at U11 is dispensable for RfaH binding when RNAP is transcribing slowly
source: Conversely, the G12C substitution eliminated the pause at U11, making measurements of RfaH antipausing activity unreliable, but did not abrogate RfaH recruitment (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that pausing at U11 is dispensable for RfaH binding when RNAP is transcribing slowly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the G12C data.

claim: RfaH induces a strong block to Exo III at U11
source: We observed that RfaH induces a strong block to Exo III at U11 (Figure 3), as expected based on previous studies (Artsimovitch and Landick, 2002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and supported by citation.

claim: RfaH was recruited to TECs halted at C9 and G10
source: RfaH was also recruited to TECs halted at C9 and G10, but not to G8 TEC in which Exo III was able to digest up to 14 bp of the upstream DNA (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: RfaH was not recruited to G8 TEC
source: RfaH was also recruited to TECs halted at C9 and G10, but not to G8 TEC in which Exo III was able to digest up to 14 bp of the upstream DNA (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: RfaH can bind to TECs halted two nucleotides ahead of the ops site
source: We conclude that RfaH can bind to TECs halted two nucleotides ahead of the ops site.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the footprinting data in Figure 3.

claim: RNAP halted at U11 can backtrack by 2–3 nt in the absence of RfaH
source: In the absence of RfaH, RNAP halted at U11 can backtrack by 2–3 nt and by one nt at G10, whereas C9 TECs are resistant to backtracking (Nedialkov et al., 2018); in all three TECs, the same region of the NT DNA will be accessible to RfaH, at least in a fraction of complexes; see Discussion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RNAP halted at G10 can backtrack by one nt in the absence of RfaH
source: In the absence of RfaH, RNAP halted at U11 can backtrack by 2–3 nt and by one nt at G10, whereas C9 TECs are resistant to backtracking (Nedialkov et al., 2018); in all three TECs, the same region of the NT DNA will be accessible to RfaH, at least in a fraction of complexes; see Discussion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: C9 TECs are resistant to backtracking
source: In the absence of RfaH, RNAP halted at U11 can backtrack by 2–3 nt and by one nt at G10, whereas C9 TECs are resistant to backtracking (Nedialkov et al., 2018); in all three TECs, the same region of the NT DNA will be accessible to RfaH, at least in a fraction of complexes; see Discussion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A crystal structure of RfaH bound to a 9-nt ops DNA (ops9) was determined at a resolution of 2.1 Å
source: To visualize the molecular details of RfaH:DNA interactions, we determined a crystal structure of RfaH bound to a 9-nt ops DNA encompassing bases G2 – G10 (ops9) at a resolution of 2.1 Å (Figure 4A, Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the RfaH:ops9 crystal contains two molecules of the complex
source: The asymmetric unit contains two molecules of the complex, in which RfaH maintains the closed, autoinhibited state typical for free RfaH (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, (Belogurov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RfaH maintains the closed, autoinhibited state in the RfaH:ops9 complex
source: The asymmetric unit contains two molecules of the complex, in which RfaH maintains the closed, autoinhibited state typical for free RfaH (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, (Belogurov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation.

claim: The DNA binds to a basic patch on RfaH-NTD opposite the RNAP/RfaH-CTD binding site
source: The DNA binds to a basic patch on RfaH-NTD opposite the RNAP/RfaH-CTD binding site and forms a hairpin structure (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The DNA forms a hairpin structure in the RfaH:ops9 complex
source: The DNA binds to a basic patch on RfaH-NTD opposite the RNAP/RfaH-CTD binding site and forms a hairpin structure (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The DNA:protein interface in the RfaH:ops9 complex encompasses 420 Å2
source: The DNA:protein interface encompasses 420 Å2.
evidence: This was calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The hairpin loop in ops9 comprises G4-A7
source: The hairpin loop comprises G4-A7, with T6 flipped out so that its nucleobase is completely exposed.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: T6 is flipped out so that its nucleobase is completely exposed in the RfaH:ops9 structure
source: The hairpin loop comprises G4-A7, with T6 flipped out so that its nucleobase is completely exposed.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: Flipped T6 inserts into a deep, narrow, positively charged pocket on RfaH-NTD
source: Flipped T6 inserts into a deep, narrow, positively charged pocket on RfaH-NTD, which is mainly formed by H20, R23, Q24, and R73 located in helices α1 and α2.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 4C.

claim: The T6 binding pocket on RfaH-NTD is mainly formed by H20, R23, Q24, and R73 located in helices α1 and α2
source: Flipped T6 inserts into a deep, narrow, positively charged pocket on RfaH-NTD, which is mainly formed by H20, R23, Q24, and R73 located in helices α1 and α2.
evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure in Figure 4C.

claim: G5 packs against the positive surface next to the T6 binding cavity
source: G5 packs against the positive surface next to this cavity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RfaH-NTD exclusively contacts nucleotides in the loop region
source: RfaH-NTD exclusively contacts nucleotides in the loop region, involving K10, H20, R23, Q24, T68, N70, A71, T72, R73, G74, and V75 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Base-specific interactions with RfaH-NTD are made by G4, G5, and T6
source: Base-specific interactions with RfaH-NTD are made by G4, G5, and T6 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B); however, only G5 and T6 form a hydrogen-bond network with RfaH-NTD that may underlie sequence-specific recognition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only G5 and T6 form a hydrogen-bond network with RfaH-NTD that may underlie sequence-specific recognition
source: Base-specific interactions with RfaH-NTD are made by G4, G5, and T6 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B); however, only G5 and T6 form a hydrogen-bond network with RfaH-NTD that may underlie sequence-specific recognition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and is an inference about the mechanism of specificity.

claim: The side chains of K10, H20, R23, and R73 directly interact with the ops DNA
source: The side chains of K10, H20, R23, and R73 directly interact with the ops DNA (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and no aromatic residues for stacking interactions are located near T6 or G5.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No aromatic residues for stacking interactions are located near T6 or G5
source: The side chains of K10, H20, R23, and R73 directly interact with the ops DNA (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and no aromatic residues for stacking interactions are located near T6 or G5.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Contacts between only two nucleobases and four amino acids mediate specific recognition of ops by RfaH
source: Thus, contacts between only two nucleobases and four amino acids mediate specific recognition of ops by RfaH.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data in Figure 4.

claim: Single Ala substitutions of each RfaH side chain that makes base-specific contacts to G5 and T6 compromise RfaH recruitment to the ops-paused TEC
source: Observations that single Ala substitutions of each RfaH side chain that makes base-specific contacts to G5 and T6 (Figure 4C) compromise RfaH recruitment to the ops-pausedTEC (Belogurov et al., 2010) argue that the RfaH:DNA contacts observed in the binary ops9:RfaH complex are functionally important.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional studies and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The stem of the DNA hairpin is formed by base pairs C3:G8 and G2:C10
source: The stem of the DNA hairpin is formed by base pairs C3:G8 and G2:C10, with T9 being flipped out.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: T9 is flipped out in the RfaH:ops9 structure
source: The stem of the DNA hairpin is formed by base pairs C3:G8 and G2:C10, with T9 being flipped out.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The G2:C10 base pair is likely an artifact of crystal packing
source: The G2:C10 base pair is likely an artifact of crystal packing as the stems of neighboring DNA molecules stack on each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and could not form in a TEC that contains a 10–11 nt bubble.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal packing shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and knowledge of TEC structure.

claim: The C3:G8 base pair is compatible with the TEC structure and may be physiologically relevant
source: In contrast, the C3:G8 base pair is compatible with the TEC structure and may be physiologically relevant.
evidence: This is an inference based on modeling and functional data.

claim: C3G and G8C substitutions reduce and abolish RfaH recruitment
source: C3G and G8C substitutions reduce and abolish RfaH recruitment (Figure 2C,D), yet these bases lack specific contacts with RfaH (Figure 4C), suggesting that a hairpin structure may be necessary.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2C, 2D, and 4C.

claim: C3 and G8 lack specific contacts with RfaH
source: C3G and G8C substitutions reduce and abolish RfaH recruitment (Figure 2C,D), yet these bases lack specific contacts with RfaH (Figure 4C), suggesting that a hairpin structure may be necessary.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A hairpin structure may be necessary for RfaH recruitment
